newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - SINGAPORE DUAL LISTING SYSTEM IN TURMOIL.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - SINGAPORE DUAL LISTING SYSTEM IN TURMOIL.

text.p: Singapore's dual listing system for a group of 16 blue chip companies was thrown into turmoil on Friday after one merged its local and foreign shares.

ST Computer Systems & Services, part of the government-linked Singapore Technologies group, made a surprise announcement that it would merge the trading of its local and foreign shares into a single tranche from Friday.

The move sparked speculation in the market that other companies with dual listings, including the Big Four Singapore banks, Singapore Airlines and Singapore Press Holdings Ltd (SPH), might follow suit.
The ST Computer announcement on Thursday night had an immediate impact. Most local shares surged to year highs at Friday's open. Foreign tranches were battered to new lows.
But the pattern reversed by noon, immediately after the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it had no intention of asking banks to merge their local and foreign share tranches.

"MAS would like to clarify that it has no intention to require banks listed on the Stock Exchange of Singapore to merge their local and foreign tranches," a spokesman for the de facto central bank told Reuters.
He said the need for dual listings depended on the company's limits on foregn shareholdings.
"Such limits are matters for companies themselves to decide," he said.
Media giant SPH issued a statement shortly afterwards to say it had no plans to change its dual listing.

SPH foreign shares bounced off a morning low of S$24.20, but were still down S$1.20 at S$26 in mid-afternoon trade. The local tranche shares slumped to a low of S$12.60 after a morning high of of S$14.30.
"Most people lost money today. Local funds who switched out of foreign shares and bought local shares were really hit," said Patrick Yau, investment analyst with Schroders.

Yau said he felt that most of the companies with dual listings were unlikely to make any changes in the near term as the change could cause havoc in the market place, wiping out billions of dollars in market capitalisation.
"Most of the foreign shares are trading at a 15-20 percent premium and some over 100 percent to their local shares," he said.
The sharp disparity has caused concern among the companies with dual listings.
"We are obviously concerned for all our shareholders and stakeholders...We have noticed the sharp premium of the foreign tranche," DBS Bank president Ng Kee Choe said on Wednesday:
But he said it was not an issue that could be decided by the bank alone.
"Whether there is a need to maintain a foreign tranche is a policy question under the (Banking) Act," he said.
Ng declined to say whether the bank had discussed the issue of maintaining foreign shares with policy makers.
Analysts said the MAS statement was also a little ambigious as it said the decision on a dual listing was up to the companies.
"MAS is just saying it is not forcing them to merge the local and foreign shares, but they have not closed the gap to that possibility," Yau said.
